findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No hemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.
echo.impression: Normal cardiac structure and function. Trace mitral regurgitation, physiological.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal examination between events and an observed event of eyelid flutter with brief unresponsiveness and immediate recovery
action_criteria.label: Examine and observe the semiology of an event
action_criteria.rationale: Her events have no limb sign to elicit; the examination documents a normal neurological examination between events and the semiology of an observed event, which guides but does not settle the diagnosis (Avbersek 2010; AAN 2025).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Sinus rhythm with normal conduction and QT interval
action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG
action_criteria.rationale: Episodes of apparent unresponsiveness: NICE advises a 12-lead ECG after transient loss of consciousness (CG109) and after a suspected seizure (NG217). The event semiology already favours functional seizures, so it does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual event recorded on video with no EEG change, normal responses to hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Video-EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation to record a habitual event
action_criteria.rationale: Events of eyelid flutter and unresponsiveness up to ten times a day, some after bright light, in a woman with childhood febrile convulsions: absence epilepsy or eyelid myoclonia is the question an EEG with hyperventilation and photic stimulation answers, and a habitual event recorded without ictal change, with normal hyperventilation and photic responses, reaches the ILAE documented level (LaFrance 2013; AAN 2025). Without the recording, the positive signs and the semiology of witnessed events support the diagnosis at a lower ILAE level of certainty (LaFrance 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Small serotonergic risk of escitalopram with sumatriptan noted; no antiseizure drug or benzodiazepine to review
action_criteria.label: Review her medicines for interactions
action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram with as-needed sumatriptan carries a small serotonergic risk; no medicine was started for the events.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Profile of the comorbid symptoms that treatment will target; it does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: A battery with performance-validity measures can quantify her anxiety and illness worry to plan treatment; it costs more than any other step on this pathway and adds nothing to the diagnosis, which rests on the examination.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background reading only; no result in it changes this patient's diagnosis or plan
action_criteria.label: Literature search on FND diagnosis and treatment (background, not a clinical step)
action_criteria.rationale: General evidence on the positive diagnosis and treatment of functional neurological disorder; it is not part of this patient's diagnostic pathway and no step of the work-up depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional seizures) based on the semiology of the habitual eyelid-flutter events, with immediate recovery, confirmed where recorded by a habitual event on video-EEG without ictal change and normal responses to hyperventilation and photic stimulation, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show how the features of the events (and the video-EEG, where recorded) support it, and give written information.
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid anxiety, including her fear of epilepsy.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.

avoided_actions.rationale: No murmur, cardiac symptom or embolic question; echocardiography answers nothing about her events.
Events of eyelid flutter for 20-40 seconds without loss of tone or pallor are not syncopal; rhythm monitoring answers no question.
A normal examination between brief eyelid-flutter events gives CT nothing to answer; it adds radiation.
No fever, meningism, encephalopathy or inflammatory question; a lumbar puncture is invasive and reinforces the search for an organic cause.
No question in her events that PET could answer.
Strength, reflexes and sensation are normal; EMG has no question to answer and a normal study reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Diffuse tingling after events without objective sensory loss is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — PNES mimicking absence seizures

differential.key_features: Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures. Febrile convulsions at age 3 and an aunt with epilepsy are weak risk factors.

Brief unresponsiveness with eyelid flutter, some after bright light, raised it, but the recorded event had no generalized spike-and-wave, and hyperventilation, photic stimulation and eye closure provoked no discharges.

key_clinical_evidence: Brief events of bilateral eyelid flutter with unresponsiveness and immediate recovery; one was observed during the examination.
No limb or sensory functional sign; the examination between events is normal.
The 24-hour video-EEG recorded a habitual 32-second event without ictal change, with no generalized spike-and-wave on hyperventilation, photic stimulation or eye closure.
Childhood febrile convulsions and a maternal aunt with epilepsy do not make the events epileptic.
Anxiety, a demanding promotion and her husband's cancer diagnosis are supportive context, neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Simple febrile convulsions add little to the later risk of epilepsy, and a second-degree relative with epilepsy does not make her events epileptic; the semiology of the events decides it, and a recorded habitual event confirms it.
red_herrings.data_point: Febrile convulsions at age 3 and a maternal aunt with adult-onset epilepsy
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic cause and start antiseizure medication before a habitual event is recorded

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. The diagnosis rests on the semiology of the events, confirmed by a habitual event recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; the anxiety is a treatment target.
red_herrings.data_point: Anxiety disorder in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions also flare with stress. A stressor is supportive context, neither required nor sufficient; the event semiology makes the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset after a promotion and her husband's prostate cancer diagnosis
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Light-triggered events raise photosensitive epilepsy, but photic stimulation produced no photoparoxysmal response and the recorded habitual event had no EEG change.
red_herrings.data_point: Some events follow exposure to bright light

findings.result: Strength 5/5 without collapsing weakness, normal reflexes, no drift, no tremor and no objective sensory loss between events.
Bilateral eyelid flutter at about 3-4 Hz with minimal head turning and unresponsiveness for 20-40 seconds, without other motor involvement, followed by immediate recovery.

clinical_assessment.impression: No motor or sensory functional sign; neurological examination otherwise normal. An event was observed (bilateral eyelid flutter with unresponsiveness for 20-40 seconds and immediate recovery); its semiology does not by itself distinguish a functional from an epileptic event.

interactions: Escitalopram + sumatriptan: combined serotonergic effect; serotonin syndrome is rare. Counsel on agitation, tremor, myoclonus, hyperreflexia and hyperthermia.
general.proposed: Escitalopram 10 mg once daily; Sumatriptan 50 mg as needed
general.summary: Escitalopram with sumatriptan carries a small serotonergic risk. No contraindicated combination.
warnings: Escitalopram: dose-related QT prolongation; hyponatremia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.

activating_procedures.eye_closure: Repeated eye closure in light and dark; no eye-closure-related discharges.
activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Two 3-minute trials; normal physiological slowing; no generalized spike-and-wave discharges and no event provoked.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: 1-30 Hz; normal photic driving; no photoparoxysmal response and no event provoked.

artifacts.description: During the event; does not obscure the posterior and central channels.

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha, symmetric, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, sleep spindles and K-complexes

findings.morphology: Bilateral eyelid flutter at about 3-4 Hz with slight head turning to the right and no response to questions, then immediate recovery. EEG showed a continuous normal background with eyelid and muscle artifact over the frontal channels; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted; no generalized spike-and-wave or other ictal pattern.
findings.type: Clinical event - eyelid flutter with unresponsiveness

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. One habitual event was recorded (bilateral eyelid flutter with unresponsiveness for 32 seconds) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the event; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the event. No generalized spike-and-wave discharges with hyperventilation, photic stimulation or eye closure. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Functional seizures that mimic absences: brief eyelid flutter with unresponsiveness, some after bright light, with childhood febrile convulsions and an aunt with epilepsy. There is no limb sign, so the diagnosis rests on the semiology of an observed event; a video-EEG with normal activation is the study that best separates the events from absences, and the agent must not start an antiseizure drug.
metadata.notes: Moderate FND — PNES mimicking absence seizures. Critical teaching: absence seizures have invariable 3 Hz spike-wave on video-EEG. Family epilepsy history is a red herring.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: criteria, outputs and assessment rebuilt to the FND criteria pack tiers. Close-out 24 Oct 2026: video-EEG optional and red-flag tests recommended, per the July 2026 agreement with the physicians that the examination is the only required diagnostic act.

patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent brief episodes of eyelid fluttering and unresponsiveness — 3 months, frequency increasing

past_medical_history: History of febrile convulsions in childhood (age 3, resolved)

social_history.recent_stressor: Work promotion to director level — performance anxiety; husband recently diagnosed with early-stage prostate cancer

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. D is a 35-year-old marketing manager who presents with 3-month history of recurrent brief episodes of bilateral eyelid fluttering and unresponsiveness. The episodes last 20-40 seconds each, occur up to 10 times per day at their worst, and have been increasing in frequency over the past month. Her husband, who has witnessed most episodes, describes them as occurring suddenly, with bilateral eyelid flutter (described as rapid blinking), slight head turning to the right, brief unresponsiveness with no ability to respond to questions, followed by immediate and complete recovery with no post-event confusion. She reports that the episodes are sometimes triggered by stress and occasionally by bright lights. She has not been injured during an episode. She has a history of febrile convulsions at age 3 (resolved) and her maternal aunt has adult-onset epilepsy treated with levetiracetam. She was started on escitalopram for anxiety approximately 8 months ago with good effect. The episodes began coincidentally approximately 3 months ago during a period of intense work stress following her promotion to marketing director, coinciding with her husband's prostate cancer diagnosis. She has not had a prior EEG. She is extremely worried that she has epilepsy given her family history and childhood febrile seizures. She denies any tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-ictal confusion with any of the episodes.

neurological_exam.additional: Intermittent episodes: bilateral eyelid fluttering, minimal head turning, unresponsive for 20-40 seconds, immediate recovery.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal at baseline. During episode: bilateral eye fluttering (3-4 Hz) without other motor involvement.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Nervous. Rapid speech.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal strength 5/5 between episodes. No give-way weakness at this time. Reflexes normal.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports diffuse tingling post-episode but no objective sensory loss on exam.
